chose: presigned PUT (signed content-type + content-length) for direct-to-bucket recipe image uploads
because: measured against the repo's own dev bucket (ghcr.io/shyim/local-s3, docker-compose.yml): presigned POST returns 403 AccessDenied, presigned PUT returns 200 and REJECTS a body of the wrong length or wrong content-type with 403. POST would make the image path the one part of the stack a laptop cannot exercise, which is the exact thing local-s3 was added to prevent. Signed content-length is also a tighter cap than content-length-range: exact bytes, not a window.

chose: drop magic-byte sniffing and the server-side SSRF image fetch; the bucket never sees server-held bytes on the write path
because: with a presigned PUT the server never holds the bytes, so there is nothing to sniff. The mime is pinned instead: the client declares it, the server refuses anything outside a fixed allowlist, and the SigV4 signature makes the declared type and byte count binding on the upload (verified: wrong type and wrong length both 403). The URL fallback went with it because it was already documented as the losing fetcher (hotlink protection blocks datacenter IPs) and it was the only remaining reason to keep putBlob, safe-fetch and a three-armed RecipeImageInput union.

the premise was that only the presign mechanism was in question. Probing further: local-s3 answers 403 to an unsigned OPTIONS, so it implements no CORS preflight at all — a browser PUT to it fails before the signature is ever checked. Direct-to-bucket upload is impossible against local-s3 by EITHER mechanism, so 'PUT because POST breaks local dev' was answering the wrong question.

chose: presigned POST (Railway's documented mechanism), and swap the dev bucket from local-s3 to MinIO so a laptop can exercise it
over: keeping local-s3 and letting browser uploads be prod-only
fronting local-s3 with a CORS-adding reverse proxy
because: measured, one client against both emulators: local-s3 refuses presigned POST (403) AND answers 403 to an unsigned OPTIONS preflight, so no direct browser upload works against it at all. MinIO does presigned POST (204), presigned GET, and sends permissive CORS preflight headers out of the box. Its POST policy enforces every bound the design needs: 2000001 bytes is EntityTooLarge, a swapped Content-Type is AccessDenied, a swapped key is AccessDenied. The repo picked local-s3 over MinIO for 'one binary, no cluster, no IAM'; MinIO server /data is also one container, and the reason it was rejected does not survive the requirement that local dev exercise the real upload path.

chose: keep recipe_pending_image.source_url, demoted to a log, by making object_key not-null rather than by deleting the column
over: dropping source_url entirely (the shape this branch shipped first)
a new migration to re-add it
because: the defect was never the column, it was that object_key was NULLABLE — that is what made 'no bytes, someone else's URL instead' a row the table would accept, and once acceptable three call sites wrote it and a read path rendered it. With object_key required, source_url cannot be a substitute for bytes, only a note about the bytes we hold. The not-null constraint is the whole difference between a log and a fallback, so that is what the schema guard now pins instead of the column list.

chose: the restored source_url log is deleted at publish, which is arguably when it becomes most interesting
couldBe: the instrument is wrong — the thing that PRODUCED this number, not the thing it describes

that is fine — the question 'where did this photo come from' is a draft-time editing concern, and after publish the bytes are the author's own blob on their own PDS, so provenance of the fetch is moot
it is a real gap — an attribution log that evaporates at publish logs nothing about the recipes people actually keep, and it should live somewhere clearPendingImage does not reach
discriminatedBy: ask whether anyone would ever query it for a PUBLISHED recipe. If yes it needs a home outside recipe_pending_image (a recipe_image column, or a recipe_meta row); if no, the current shape is complete.
